::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[How to solve the above differential equation?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4754940/how-to-solve-the-above-differential-equation), asked by [SUBHA SANKAR ROY](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1195138/subha-sankar-roy) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2023-08-18; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> $$\frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{y}{x}$$
>
> How to solve this differential equation? I know how to solve this because the ultimate way of solving this is $y\,dy=x\,dx$ and then integrating on both sides we will get $y^2/2=x^2/2 +c$. But my question is that why we don't put constants on both sides of the equation like I am trying to say that why the solution is not $y^2/2 + C =x^2/2 +c$? Why do we don't put constants on both sides?
:::

You could do that, but the next step would be to collect both arbitrary constants to one side of the equation. One arbitrary additive constant on one side is no more or less arbitrary that one on each side. So there is no loss of generality in just using one.

The value(s) of the constant(s) are determined by the initial conditions of the differential equation you are trying to solve. If you added two constants, you would see that one is determined by initial conditions and one is determined by the other constant. So two constants don't generalize your solution any further; they only encumber it.
